subject: Suggestions for an alternative population estimation technique

messages.author: 6919d512766fa133
messages.subject: Suggestions for an alternative population estimation technique
parts:
Dear All,

This mail is to find out suggestions for a possible technique suitable
for the population estimation of Nilgiri tahr (Hemitragus hylocrius
Ogilby), a mountain goat in the Eravikulam National Park. The Park is
situated in the High Ranges of the Western Ghats in India. It covers
an area of about 97 sq km and is of undulating terrain comprising a
high rolling plateau with a base elevation of about 2000 m. Most of
the peaks rise 100-300 m above this plateau. The horizontally and
vertically rounded cliffs are the characteristic features of the Park.
The terrain is covered primarily with the grasslands and small
patches of forest in gullies and hollows.=A0 Shrub lands are found along
the bases of cliffs and intersperse in rocky areas.

Nilgiri tahr lives in herds and sensitive to the presence of human.
The preferred habitats of the tahr are rocky outcrops set amongst
grass hills and cliffs bordering grasslands to escape from predators.

The tahr population in the Park is usually estimated by the Park
Mangers using bounded count technique (Regier and Robson,1966). Twelve
blocks based on the home range, were taken as the basic units for the
population estimation. Although bounded count is rarely used for
terrestrial animal species, application of this method several times
in the past reveals that it does provide the reasonable estimates of
the tahr population.

However, there are suggestions that other techniques should be tried
because the bounded count does not involve probability of animal
detection.

Placing line transects is very difficult in the highly undulating
terrain. Therefore, the line transect sampling is not suitable.

Anyone would like to suggest a technique which we can attempt to
estimate the population of this endangered species?.


Reference:

Regier, H.A. and D.S. Robson (1966). Estimating population numbers and
=A0 mortality=A0=A0 rates.=A0 In: S.D. Gerking (ed.). The biological basis =
of
fresh water fish production.=A0 Blackwell Scientific Publication,
Oxford, U.K.


M.Sivaram
Scientist
Kerala Forest Research Institute
Peechi - 680653
Kerala State
India

messages.author: 3bbe9e00c88a70b2
messages.subject: Re: Suggestions for an alternative population estimation technique
parts:
If (and this is a big if) you can mark a random sample of tahr, which=20
can be visually identified to the individual during resightings, then=20
you might want to consider the Bowden estimator (Bowden and Kufeld=20
1995). The advantage of this estimator is that your resighting effort=20
can be unequally distributed in both a spatial and temporal manner=20
(during a time period in which the population is closed). If you have=20
sufficient sample sizes there are equivalent likelihood based estimators=20
(McClintock et al. 2006, 2008) that permit you to model covariates for=20
detection probabilities. Although the paper was written with bird=20
surveys in mind, I have a paper that provides some guidelines on marked=20
sample sizes and resighting effort (Diefenbach 2009).

Bowden, D. C., and R. C. Kufeld. 1995. Generalized mark=96sight populatio=
n=20
size estimation applied to Colorado moose. Journal of Wildlife=20
Management 59:840=96851.

Diefenbach, D. R. 2009. Estimating avian population size using Bowden's=20
estimator. Auk 126:211-217.

McClintock, B. T., G. C. White, and K. P. Burnham. 2006. A robust design=20
mark=96resight abundance estimator allowing heterogeneity in sighting=20
probabilities. Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental=20
Statistics 11:231=96248.

McClintock, B. T., G. C. White, K. P. Burnham, and M. A. Pryde. 2008. A=20
generalized mixed effects model of abundance for mark=96sight data when=20
sampling is without replacement. Pages 273=96292 in Modeling Demographic=20
Processes in Marked Populations (D. L. Thomson, E. G. Cooch, and M. J.=20
Conroy, Eds.). Springer, New York.

Regards,

Duane Diefenbach

messages.author: 6427498a73d3de53
messages.subject: Re: Suggestions for an alternative population estimation technique
parts: A colleague has motivated me to subscribe and follow up on Duane's excell=

ent comments. Mark-resight has often been used for mountain sheep under =
similar conditions (e.g., Neal et al. 1993). Some other mark-resight pap=
ers you may find useful are White & Shenk (2001) and McClintock & White (=
2009, 2010). A nice thing about some of the newer models is that they do=
n't require that one know the exact number of marked individuals that are=
alive and within the study area during surveys (this can be difficult to=
accomplish without transmitters!).
McClintock BT, and GC White (2009) A less field-intensive robust design f=

or estimating demographic parameters with mark-resight data. Ecology 90:3=
13=E2=80=93320.
McClintock BT, and GC White (2010) From NOREMARK to MARK: software for es=
timating demographic parameters using mark-resight methodology. Journal =

of Ornithology doi:10.1007/s10336-010-0524-x.

Neal, AK, GC White, RB Gill, DF Reed, and JH Olterman. 1993. Evaluation o=

f mark=E2=80=93resight model assumptions for estimating mountain sheep nu=
mbers. Journal of Wildlife Management 57:436=E2=80=93450.

White GC, and TM Shenk (2001) Population estimation with radiomarked anim=
als. In: Millspaugh J, Marzluff JM (eds) Radio
tracking and animal populations. Academic, San Diego, pp 329=E2=80=93350.=

Cheers,
Brett McClintock

messages.author: 6919d512766fa133
messages.subject: Re: Suggestions for an alternative population estimation technique
parts:
I am thankful to Duane and Brett for their suggestions and valuable
references . Your suggestions indeed led to some serious discussions
with my colleagues.We are in the opinion that it is not practically
possible to mark tahr for re-sighting. Tahr moves mostly in herds and
in open grass lands. We are thinking whether we can use digital
photographing of herds in different days with sufficient intervals for
re-sighting the herds/individuals by closely reading the animal/herd's
features and then use mark-resight models. I am not aware of anybody
using photographing method for animals which move in herds. Of course,
it is now a days used for the population estimation of tiger
(solitary).

M.Sivaram
Scientist
Kerala Forest Research Institute
Peechi - 680653
Kerala State
India
